title: Mauve, the accidental colour
hook: A teenager trying to make medicine at home invented the first synthetic dye instead.
peek: In 1856, 18-year-old William Perkin was trying to make quinine from coal tar chemicals in his home lab. He failed, but found a purple that dyed silk beautifully. Mauve became a fashion craze and started the synthetic dye industry.
lede: Over the Easter holiday in 1856, an 18-year-old chemistry student named William Henry Perkin was experimenting in a makeshift lab at home in London. He was trying to make quinine, a valuable medicine, from chemicals found in coal tar. It did not work. But one dark leftover dissolved into a vivid purple that dyed silk well and did not wash out.

bullets.text: Perkin was oxidising aniline, a coal tar chemical. His aniline was not pure, and chemists later found that the impurities were part of what made the purple form. A cleaner sample might have given him nothing.
Perkin patented the dye, left college and, with his father and brother, built a factory at Greenford, near London. He had become a successful industrialist while still a young man.

The colour took off when fashionable women, including Queen Victoria and the French Empress Eugénie, wore it. By the late 1850s the craze was known as mauve mania, after the French name for the mallow flower.
Perkin sold the business in his thirties and went back to research. He was knighted in 1906, fifty years after the discovery, and the anniversary was celebrated by chemists in Britain and abroad.
